clue.text: What’s the point when the author has finished a bit of writing?

definitions.text: What’s the point when the author has finished a bit of writing?

blocks.note: surface reading: a weary writer asking why bother once the work is done

blocks.clueFragment: when the author has finished a bit of writing
blocks.note: setter's reading: the point is a literal dot of punctuation placed at the end of a sentence

explanation.walkthrough: 'What's the point' reads as an idiom of despair, but the point is a printed dot. In British English the dot ending a sentence is called a full stop; Americans say period.
explanation.definitionFit: The punctuation mark that closes a sentence is a dot, literally a point, put there once the sentence is complete.

clue.text: Make fun of conclusive act

definitions.note: a verb phrase; the verb is written as two words, the hyphenated form is the noun

blocks.note: first meaning: to tease someone, British slang
second meaning: the final stage that brings something to an end

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang to wind someone up is to tease or provoke them; the noun a wind-up is such a tease, and also the finishing of business.
explanation.definitionFit: Winding up means bringing proceedings to a close, so the noun names the closing stage; the phrasal verb is British slang for teasing.

clue.text: King having a hot rum poured out in African city

indicators.note: liquid poured out spills and lands in a new shape, so the letters are spilled into a new order

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monarch is served a hot rum toddy while visiting an African city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poured out' suggests serving the drink, but it tells you to spill the letters; the king stays put at the front as his chess abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan, standing where the Blue and White Niles meet.

clue.text: Mum with nothing looking down on a foreign capital

indicators.note: in a down clue whatever looks down on something sits above it, so the parts stack in order

blocks.note: Ma is an informal word for mother
nil means nothing, as in a football score
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mother with nothing to her name gazes down on a foreign city.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a down clue, so 'looking down on' places each piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Manila is the capital city of the Philippines, so from a British setter's viewpoint it is a foreign seat of government.

clue.text: Penny maybe hugs American relative

indicators.note: a hug wraps arms around someone, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: a penny is one example of a coin
US is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A woman called Penny embraces a relative over from America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a woman's name, but 'maybe' marks it as an example of something else: a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A cousin is a child of one's aunt or uncle, a family member and so a relative.

clue.text: A bit cracked, in more ways than one?

blocks.note: first reading: slightly mad, since cracked is slang for crazy
setter's reading: also literally covered in fine cracks, as old glazed pottery or varnish becomes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' is slang for mad, and the answer means mad too; the tag 'in more ways than one' says it also describes a surface with a network of fine cracks.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazing is the web of hairline fractures on old glaze, and someone deranged is also described by the same past participle.

clue.text: Battles may be reported in this combination of words

indicators.note: a report is spoken news, so what comes next is the sound of a word rather than its spelling

blocks.note: frays are fights or skirmishes

explanation.surface: Wartime battles may be described in a particular form of words.
explanation.walkthrough: A fray is a fight, so battles are frays, which said out loud match the spelt answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase is a small group of words forming a unit within a sentence, such as an idiom or expression.

clue.text: Messages that could bring a smile

indicators.note: 'could bring' suggests something that can be produced from given material, so the letters are reworked into a fresh word

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Some messages arrive that cheer the reader up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a pleasant comment on receiving notes; the six letters of A SMILE are the ones rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Electronic notes sent through the internet are digital messages, so the plural answer matches the plural definition.

clue.text: Maiden, possibly former lover, quoted as being too emotional

blocks.note: in cricket a maiden is a kind of over, one in which no runs are scored
an ex is a former partner
to cite is to quote

explanation.surface: A young woman, perhaps a former girlfriend, is said to be getting far too worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' suggests a young woman, but it is cricket: a maiden over is a set of six balls bowled with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone worked up past a sensible level of agitation is too emotional, the prefix supplying the sense of excess.

clue.text: Jack was ill, stuck in prison

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
to ail is to be unwell

explanation.surface: A man called Jack fell sick while serving a prison sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a man's name, but it is the playing card, abbreviated J.
explanation.definitionFit: A person locked up behind bars by the courts is confined in a cell, the past participle matching the adjectival phrase.

clue.text: Upright vicar let rip

indicators.note: to rip is to tear apart, and torn pieces land in a jumbled new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An upstanding clergyman finally loses his temper and lets loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright' seems to describe the vicar's morals, but it is the definition; 'let' joins the fodder while 'rip' alone signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something standing straight up, at right angles to the horizon, is upright in the literal positional sense.

clue.text: Touched material

blocks.note: first meaning: past tense of handling something with the fingers
second meaning: a fabric made of pressed and matted wool

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two separate meanings of one short word: a past tense verb and a cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of the verb for sensing by hand doubles as the name of a dense non-woven textile.

clue.text: Fellow in Bible story not doomed to punishment

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a parable is a moral story, such as those told by Jesus
a fellow of an Oxford or Cambridge college is a don

explanation.surface: A man in a biblical tale escapes the punishment he seemed bound for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' looks like any man, but it is the academic sense: a college fellow, or don.
explanation.definitionFit: An offence that can be forgiven is excusable, so whoever committed it need not face a penalty.

clue.text: Rough map pirate unfolded containing old symbol for treasure location

indicators.note: something unfolded is opened out of its usual shape, so the letters are spread into a new order
to contain is to hold within, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old
X marks the spot on a treasure map

explanation.surface: A pirate spreads out a rough chart showing the traditional mark for where the treasure is buried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' sits at the front as if describing the chart, but it is the definition. X is the traditional mark on a treasure map.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough estimate or sketch is not exact, only close to the truth, the same sense as the adjective answer.

clue.text: Someone having accommodation in desert after wandering

indicators.note: wandering means drifting off course, so the letters stray into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nomad finds somewhere to stay in the desert after roaming about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word placing someone in the desert, but its letters belong to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who lives in a particular house or place, occupying lodgings there, is an inhabitant of it.

clue.text: Meat cooked repeatedly for fellow in the side

indicators.note: repeatedly means more than once, so the same word is written twice in a row
cooking transforms raw ingredients, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the word written down twice

explanation.surface: Meat is cooked again and again for a sporting colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: Two copies of MEAT give eight letters to rearrange. A side is a sports team, a common British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A fellow member of the same sports team, the side, is a colleague playing alongside you.

clue.text: Litter in distant line of terraced houses?

blocks.note: far means distant
terraced houses are joined in a row, so a row is one example of such a line

explanation.surface: Rubbish has piled up along a faraway street of joined houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' suggests rubbish, but it means a batch of young animals. Terraced houses are British houses built joined in a continuous row.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrow is a litter of piglets born to a sow at one time, a specialised farming sense of the noun.

clue.text: The case of an archer making one tremble

blocks.note: first meaning: the container an archer carries arrows in
second meaning: to shake slightly

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a nervous archer, but 'case' is a literal holder for arrows, and the trembling is the word's second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the archer's arrow holder, and the same word as a verb means to shake with a slight rapid motion.

clue.text: Fiery striker in game’s given sign of approval

blocks.note: a match is a game, and the apostrophe S is kept
a tick mark shows something is correct or approved

explanation.surface: A hot-headed footballer in the match is given a nod of approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiery striker' suggests a temperamental centre forward, but the striker is something struck to make fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin wooden stick tipped with chemicals is struck against a box to light it, so it bursts into flame.

clue.text: Mammals one’s hidden in garments

indicators.note: whatever is tucked away inside something else sits within it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: coats are garments
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Some animal is tucked away inside pieces of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'one' stands for 'is', so the instruction reads 'one is tucked inside garments'.
explanation.definitionFit: Coatis are raccoon-like animals of the Americas with long ringed tails, warm-blooded furry creatures.

clue.text: Catherine engages artist in contact sport

indicators.note: to engage is to take on or hold, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: Kate is a short form of Catherine
RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A woman named Catherine takes on a painter in a physical sport.
explanation.walkthrough: RA is a crossword staple for an artist, from the Royal Academy in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Karate is a Japanese martial art of strikes and kicks, a combat discipline in which opponents touch each other.

clue.text: Neighbour – a target of ridicule, we hear

definitions.note: a verb here: to lie next to

indicators.note: hearing takes in sound, so what matters is how the words are spoken

blocks.note: a butt is someone others make fun of, the butt of the joke

explanation.surface: The person next door is a laughing stock, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neighbour' reads as a noun, but it is the verb: to neighbour something is to adjoin it.
explanation.definitionFit: Two properties that share a boundary border each other, and to border is to adjoin, the verb sense needed.

clue.text: Material to fade behind church instrument?

indicators.note: being behind means coming after, so the parts follow one another in that order

blocks.note: the organ is the instrument found in most churches
a sound or light dies away when it fades

explanation.surface: Fabric hung behind the church organ is losing its colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fade' suggests colour draining from cloth, but here it means die away.
explanation.definitionFit: Organdie, spelt organdy in America, is a fine stiffened cotton fabric used for dresses and trimmings.

clue.text: Get rid of this writer going the wrong way in ramble

indicators.note: travelling the wrong way means heading backwards, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the setter refers to themselves, so 'this writer' is me
to rove is to wander or ramble

explanation.surface: A walker who has taken a wrong turn on a hike wants to be rid of the writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter's way of saying ME. Ramble is a verb here, to wander.
explanation.definitionFit: To take something away so it is no longer there is to eliminate it, the plain sense of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Sound of horse – for what reason? – outside pub

indicators.note: to be outside is to surround, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: why asks for a reason
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: Someone wonders why a horse is neighing outside a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'for what reason?' an aside; it is a phrase meaning why, which goes around the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle high-pitched neigh is the noise a horse makes, especially when calling or excited.

clue.text: Old coin, say, with head of Rex or Regina

indicators.note: the head of something is its top or start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: to state is to say
both Latin words for the monarch begin with the same letter

explanation.surface: An ancient coin, for example, bearing the portrait of a king or queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' suggests the monarch's portrait on a coin, but it only takes the first letter; Rex and Regina, king and queen, conveniently share it.
explanation.definitionFit: The stater was a gold or silver coin used in ancient Greece and its colonies, so it is a historic piece of currency.
